query:
Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer. The charge is induction-melted in a graphite
crucible (grade not yet confirmed, probably a fine-grained isostatic graphite) whose interior is sprayed
with a boron nitride release coating, then pushed by argon pressure through a bottom hBN nozzle. The alloy
is nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 (Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%) melted at 1300 C under argon, in charges of
0.86-1.08 kg.

The coating is Momentive Technologies "Boron Nitride Spray II, High-Temperature Release Coating"
(material number 2111750, 13 oz / 369 g aerosol can). Its SDS, as we read it (please verify), lists
hexagonal BN in ethanol and acetone, LPG (propane/butane) propellant and 1-5% organoclay (a
bentonite-based rheology additive), so the dry film is BN platelets with very little binder. Momentive
rates a can for roughly 100 sq ft.

History:
- Coat 1 (before a 27 Oct run): sprayed onto the clean, bare graphite and left to dry. It did NOT crack.
  It was not baked before use: the chamber filled with smoke at about 500 C during the first heat-up,
  with the metal charge already loaded (binder burnout in the furnace).
- After that run a thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling it
  pulled away crescent-shaped patches of the BN coat, leaving bare graphite. A second run used the
  crucible with those bare patches, without recoating.
- Coat 2 (30 Oct): the crucible was re-sprayed with the same product and left to dry in a laboratory fume
  hood. When the operator came back, the coat was cracked. It cracked at room temperature during drying,
  before any heating. We do not yet know: whether the old fired coat was fully stripped or the new coat
  went over it (or over the patch edges); how many passes, how far from the surface, or how long the can
  was shaken; whether the crucible had just been wiped with isopropanol (our recoat notes say to wipe with
  IPA and never water); the room humidity; the crack pattern (polygonal "mud-crack" network, curling
  flakes, or single long cracks); and whether only the coat cracked or the graphite too.

Please answer as a literature review with numbers and sources (papers with DOIs, manufacturer data sheets
and application instructions). Mark every estimate as an estimate and show its inputs. Start with a
short ranked list of the most likely causes, then cover:

1. Mechanism. Explain drying cracks in sprayed particulate coatings: capillary pressure in the drying
   particle network, constraint by the substrate, and the critical cracking thickness (for example Chiu
   et al. 1993 in J. Am. Ceram. Soc.; Routh and Russel; Tirumkudulu and Russel 2005; Singh and
   Tirumkudulu 2007; Lee and Routh; work on films of platelet particles). How do particle size, packing, platelet shape and
   orientation (hBN platelets of about 0.5-10 um), a few percent clay or organic binder, solvent surface
   tension (acetone and ethanol, about 22-23 mN/m) and drying rate change the critical thickness? Estimate
   the critical cracking thickness of a hBN-platelet film with 1-5% organoclay, and compare it with the
   wet and dry thickness an aerosol deposits per pass. How many grams of spray per square centimetre give
   what dry thickness? Is a dry BN film of 50-150 um above or below the critical thickness?
2. Substrate and history. Why would the same spray crack on a crucible that had already been coated and
   fired, when it did not crack on bare graphite? Consider: a porous, binder-free fired BN layer (or
   residual borate or B2O3) that wicks the solvent and consolidates the new film from below; poor adhesion
   or a weak boundary layer under the new film; locally doubled thickness where new spray overlaps old
   coat or fills the bare crescents; residues from the skull (Al2O3, metal, reaction products); solvent or
   moisture left in porous graphite or in the old coat after an IPA wipe; hydration of B2O3 or borate in
   the fired coat to boric acid; and porosity or surface texture of the graphite. Which of these are
   supported by literature or vendor guidance, and which are speculation?
3. Drying conditions. What does strong airflow (a fume hood face velocity of about 0.3-0.5 m/s) do to an
   acetone/ethanol BN film: faster evaporation, skin formation, lateral drying fronts, evaporative cooling
   below the dew point with water condensing into the film ("blushing"), and non-uniform drying in a deep
   cup? Would slower drying (still air, a lid, or gentle warming) avoid cracking? Quantify where you can.
4. Spray technique. Effects of insufficient shaking (BN settles quickly), spray distance, can and part
   temperature, a nearly empty can (lower propellant pressure giving a wetter, coarser spray), spraying
   into a deep cylindrical crucible (overspray pooling on the bottom and in the corner), and the number of
   passes and the flash time between them. Collect vendor instructions with numbers from Momentive, ZYP
   Coatings (BN Lubricoat and Hardcoat aerosols), Saint-Gobain (Combat), Henze (HeBoCoat), 3M and others,
   especially statements that cracking, flaking or peeling means the coat is too thick, and their advice
   on recoating over an existing or fired coat versus stripping it first.
5. Momentive Boron Nitride Spray II specifically. What do Momentive's technical data sheet, SDS and
   application notes say about composition, binder, thickness per coat, drying time, whether to bake
   before contact with metal, maximum use temperature in air and in inert gas, and recoating? Is another
   product (Momentive's water-based BN paints, or a hard-coat BN with an inorganic binder) better suited
   to repeated recoating of a graphite crucible for an aluminum-containing copper melt at 1300 C?
6. Consequences and diagnosis. How do you tell drying mud-cracks in the coat from cracks in the graphite
   (for example thermal-shock cracks that show through) or old cracks telegraphing through the new coat?
   Is a finely mud-cracked but adherent BN release coat acceptable for a 1300 C aluminum bronze melt, or
   does the melt penetrate the cracks, reach the graphite (Al4C3, carbon pickup, skull adhesion) and lift
   flakes into the melt and the nozzle? Must it be stripped?
7. Fix. Give a step-by-step strip, recoat, dry and inspect procedure for this product on a graphite
   crucible that avoids cracking: how to strip a cracked or fired BN coat without water, surface
   preparation, passes, thickness per pass and in total, flash time, where and how to dry, an optional
   low-temperature warm-up and the burnout or bake before the first melt, and pass/fail inspection
   criteria. Also propose a small coupon test (graphite offcuts) that would identify which factor caused
   the cracking, for example clean graphite versus a fired coat, fume-hood draft versus still air, and
   one versus three versus six passes, with weighing to estimate thickness.
task_summary: Literature Review Of Drying Cracks And Recoating Procedures For Boron Nitride Spray On Graphite

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer. The charge is induction-melted in a graphite
crucible (grade not yet confirmed, probably a fine-grained isostatic graphite) whose interior is sprayed
with a boron nitride release coating, then pushed by argon pressure through a bottom hBN nozzle. The alloy
is nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 (Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%) melted at 1300 C under argon, in charges of
0.86-1.08 kg.

The coating is Momentive Technologies "Boron Nitride Spray II, High-Temperature Release Coating"
(material number 2111750, 13 oz / 369 g aerosol can). Its SDS, as we read it (please verify), lists
hexagonal BN in ethanol and acetone, LPG (propane/butane) propellant and 1-5% organoclay (a
bentonite-based rheology additive), so the dry film is BN platelets with very little binder. Momentive
rates a can for roughly 100 sq ft.

History:
- Coat 1 (before a 27 Oct run): sprayed onto the clean, bare graphite and left to dry. It did NOT crack.
  It was not baked before use: the chamber filled with smoke at about 500 C during the first heat-up,
  with the metal charge already loaded (binder burnout in the furnace).
- After that run a thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling it
  pulled away crescent-shaped patches of the BN coat, leaving bare graphite. A second run used the
  crucible with those bare patches, without recoating.
- Coat 2 (30 Oct): the crucible was re-sprayed with the same product and left to dry in a laboratory fume
  hood. When the operator came back, the coat was cracked. It cracked at room temperature during drying,
  before any heating. We do not yet know: whether the old fired coat was fully stripped or the new coat
  went over it (or over the patch edges); how many passes, how far from the surface, or how long the can
  was shaken; whether the crucible had just been wiped with isopropanol (our recoat notes say to wipe with
  IPA and never water); the room humidity; the crack pattern (polygonal "mud-crack" network, curling
  flakes, or single long cracks); and whether only the coat cracked or the graphite too.

Please answer as a literature review with numbers and sources (papers with DOIs, manufacturer data sheets
and application instructions). Mark every estimate as an estimate and show its inputs. Start with a
short ranked list of the most likely causes, then cover:

1. Mechanism. Explain drying cracks in sprayed particulate coatings: capillary pressure in the drying
   particle network, constraint by the substrate, and the critical cracking thickness (for example Chiu
   et al. 1993 in J. Am. Ceram. Soc.; Routh and Russel; Tirumkudulu and Russel 2005; Singh and
   Tirumkudulu 2007; Lee and Routh; work on films of platelet particles). How do particle size, packing, platelet shape and
   orientation (hBN platelets of about 0.5-10 um), a few percent clay or organic binder, solvent surface
   tension (acetone and ethanol, about 22-23 mN/m) and drying rate change the critical thickness? Estimate
   the critical cracking thickness of a hBN-platelet film with 1-5% organoclay, and compare it with the
   wet and dry thickness an aerosol deposits per pass. How many grams of spray per square centimetre give
   what dry thickness? Is a dry BN film of 50-150 um above or below the critical thickness?
2. Substrate and history. Why would the same spray crack on a crucible that had already been coated and
   fired, when it did not crack on bare graphite? Consider: a porous, binder-free fired BN layer (or
   residual borate or B2O3) that wicks the solvent and consolidates the new film from below; poor adhesion
   or a weak boundary layer under the new film; locally doubled thickness where new spray overlaps old
   coat or fills the bare crescents; residues from the skull (Al2O3, metal, reaction products); solvent or
   moisture left in porous graphite or in the old coat after an IPA wipe; hydration of B2O3 or borate in
   the fired coat to boric acid; and porosity or surface texture of the graphite. Which of these are
   supported by literature or vendor guidance, and which are speculation?
3. Drying conditions. What does strong airflow (a fume hood face velocity of about 0.3-0.5 m/s) do to an
   acetone/ethanol BN film: faster evaporation, skin formation, lateral drying fronts, evaporative cooling
   below the dew point with water condensing into the film ("blushing"), and non-uniform drying in a deep
   cup? Would slower drying (still air, a lid, or gentle warming) avoid cracking? Quantify where you can.
4. Spray technique. Effects of insufficient shaking (BN settles quickly), spray distance, can and part
   temperature, a nearly empty can (lower propellant pressure giving a wetter, coarser spray), spraying
   into a deep cylindrical crucible (overspray pooling on the bottom and in the corner), and the number of
   passes and the flash time between them. Collect vendor instructions with numbers from Momentive, ZYP
   Coatings (BN Lubricoat and Hardcoat aerosols), Saint-Gobain (Combat), Henze (HeBoCoat), 3M and others,
   especially statements that cracking, flaking or peeling means the coat is too thick, and their advice
   on recoating over an existing or fired coat versus stripping it first.
5. Momentive Boron Nitride Spray II specifically. What do Momentive's technical data sheet, SDS and
   application notes say about composition, binder, thickness per coat, drying time, whether to bake
   before contact with metal, maximum use temperature in air and in inert gas, and recoating? Is another
   product (Momentive's water-based BN paints, or a hard-coat BN with an inorganic binder) better suited
   to repeated recoating of a graphite crucible for an aluminum-containing copper melt at 1300 C?
6. Consequences and diagnosis. How do you tell drying mud-cracks in the coat from cracks in the graphite
   (for example thermal-shock cracks that show through) or old cracks telegraphing through the new coat?
   Is a finely mud-cracked but adherent BN release coat acceptable for a 1300 C aluminum bronze melt, or
   does the melt penetrate the cracks, reach the graphite (Al4C3, carbon pickup, skull adhesion) and lift
   flakes into the melt and the nozzle? Must it be stripped?
7. Fix. Give a step-by-step strip, recoat, dry and inspect procedure for this product on a graphite
   crucible that avoids cracking: how to strip a cracked or fired BN coat without water, surface
   preparation, passes, thickness per pass and in total, flash time, where and how to dry, an optional
   low-temperature warm-up and the burnout or bake before the first melt, and pass/fail inspection
   criteria. Also propose a small coupon test (graphite offcuts) that would identify which factor caused
   the cracking, for example clean graphite versus a fired coat, fume-hood draft versus still air, and
   one versus three versus six passes, with weighing to estimate thickness.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this complex question about BN coating cracking on graphite crucibles for aluminum bronze atomization.

    title = "Influence of drying conditions on the stress and weight development of capillary suspensions",
    year = "2020",
    journal = "Journal of the American Ceramic Society",
    volume = "104",

    issn = "0002-7820"

Abstract:
Cracking of suspensions during drying is a common problem. While additives, e.g. binders and surfactants, can mitigate this problem, some applications, such as printing conductive pastes or sintering green bodies, do not lend themselves to the use of additives. Capillary suspensions provide an alternative formulation without additives. In this work, we use simultaneous stress and weight measurements to investigate the influence of formulation and drying conditions. Capillary suspensions dry more homogeneously and with lower peak stresses, leading to an increased robustness against cracking compared. An increase in dry film porosity is not the key driver for the stress reduction. Instead, the capillary bridges, which create strong particle networks, resist the stress. Increasing the relative humidity enhances this effect, even for pure suspensions. While lower boiling point secondary liquids, e.g. water, persist for very long times during drying, higher boiling point liquids offer further potential to tune the the drying process.

Abstract:
Thin films of polymer coatings have important industrial applications ranging from paints and coatings to pharmaceuticals. In many applications, the coatings are obtained by applying thin films of dilute polymer solutions, wherein the solvent evaporates to leave behind a thin polymer film. In some cases, the thin films may crack due to shrinkage stresses developed during drying. While a number of studies have focused on the stress development, the phenomenon of cracking in polymer films is not fully investigated. In the present work, thin films of a silicone polymer solution were cast on substrates of varying Young's moduli and investigated for cracking as a function of film thickness and substrate modulus. Micro-Raman spectroscopy measurements show that thin films dry uniformly while thick films form a skin at the top surface leading to slow drying rates. Transverse stresses were measured using the cantilever technique and related to the extent of cracking in the film. We investigated the influence of substrate rigidity on the cracking behavior and found that decreasing the stiffness of the substrate increases the extent of cracking.

Abstract:
<jats:p>We report a systematic investigation of GME (1-glyceryl monooleyl ether) self-assembly of TiO₂–water–butanediol quaternary colloidal suspensions and its consequences for crack formation during film drying. Because 1,4-butanediol has a boiling point of ~230°C and a vapour pressure orders of magnitude below that of water, drying progressively enriches the GME–butanediol–water phase in both co-solvent and surfactant rather than depleting it of a volatile additive. Cross-polarised optical microscopy (POM) established that lamellar or hexagonal lyotropic liquid-crystalline (LC) phases form at ≥2 wt% GME in butanediol:water 1:20 mixtures, and at ≥2 wt% GME in 3:7 mixtures. UNIFAC-based drying-path simulations confirmed that water evaporates preferentially, predicting that 3:7 BDO/H₂O formulations at ≥2 wt% GME cross into the lamellar LC window when ≈72 ± 4% of the initial water remains. Critical cracking thickness (hᴄᴄᴛ) measurements on TiO₂ films (≈200 nm, 3.5 vol%) demonstrated a 2.3-fold increase from 17.5 ± 0.6 µm (additive-free control) to 41.4 ± 2.9 µm at 3:7 BDO/3 wt% GME at 25°C (p < 0.001, one-way ANOVA). The enhancement is primarily LC-mediated: the apparent shear modulus Gₐₚₚ of the LC phase (exp(0.71ϕf)) elevates the Tirumkudulu–Russel fracture-resistance prefactor by a factor of ≈1.7× (model R² = 0.993). Residual butanediol in dried films (9.4 ± 0.6 wt% at the 3:7/2 wt% GME condition) contributes a secondary plasticisation effect (r² = 0.62 vs. r² = 0.91 for the LC contribution). Isomer comparison confirmed that 1,4-butanediol (hᴄᴄᴛ = 34.0 µm) outperforms 1,3-butanediol (29.7 µm) and 2,3-butanediol (27.2 µm), consistent with the linear backbone geometry of 1,4-BDO favouring GME lamellar packing. These results demonstrate a low-volatility, low-VOC additive route to crack-free thick particulate coatings and offer a mechanistic framework for non-volatile co-solvent–amphiphile systems in particulate film drying.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract The aim of this study is to assess the effectiveness of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) coatings to enhance the corrosion resistance of metals as well as evaluate their crucial toxicological impacts on both the environment and human health. Organic coatings are extensively applied in the field of protecting metals against corrosion. They are preferred as corrosion inhibitors due to their carbonyl and hydroxyl group content, but they have drawbacks regarding brittleness, porosity, and oxidation susceptibility. In this review, we mainly focused on the synthesis, properties, and applications of hBN coatings and emphasized the way to improve corrosion resistance in metals and alloys. Furthermore, our discussion demonstrated that the boron nitride nanosheet (BNNS) coatings significantly improve corrosion resistance, hydrophobicity, and crack mitigation properties. The researchers achieved reduced coating porosity and enhanced protection against corrosive media by effectively dispersing BNNS in organic resin. This study also determines the protective mechanism of BNNS composite coatings against corrosion. Moreover, we addressed the impact of BBNS synthesis and its physicochemical properties on the environment and organisms. Finally, suggestions are made for future research and the sustainability of industrial use to broaden the scope of applications for BNNS composite coating.

Abstract:
In contrast to a mass of powder in air at 900 °C, the oxidation rate of hexagonal boron nitride does not tend to a plateau when present as a coating on austenitic stainless steel type 304 and type 310, and a real‐world hot forming tool alloy. As with a mass of powder, a molten boron trioxide diffusion barrier encapsulates each hexagonal boron nitride grain around the basal plane. These subsequently merge to form a dispersion of remnant grains throughout a molten matrix. Boron trioxide is semipermeable, and as such, the substrate oxidizes concurrently. As it does so, outwardly diffusing chromium (III) ions react with boron trioxide to form chromium borate, which depletes the diffusion barrier. This causes the oxidation of hexagonal boron nitride to be sustained at an enhanced rate and the overlayer ultimately undergoes complete decomposition. During this process, the scale comprises chromium borate and chromia only. While manganese chromium spinel and iron chromium spinel form readily at the oxide‐atmosphere interface of equivalently heat‐treated uncoated substrates, they do not form until after the coating has completely decomposed.

Abstract:
Polycrystalline cBN/copper composite abrasive particles were prepared by an electroless powder coating process. Ti metallization and tin/silver metallization techniques were used to improve the coating process by depositing an autocatalytic metallic layer on the surface of the cBN particles. Metallized, as well as un-metallized, cBN particles were further coated by copper using electroless deposition. Electroless copper coating of un-metallized and metallized cBN particles by 90 wt.% of copper were achieved. The surface morphology, the composition and the crystalline phase identifications of the metallized cBN particles, as well as the 10 wt.% cBN /copper composite powders, were investigated by field emission scanning electron microscopy, an energy-dispersive spectrometer and an X-ray diffractometer. The results show that the surface of the Ti metalized and tin/Ag-metallized cBN particles were covered by the nanosized Ti or Ag layer, respectively, which enhanced the deposition of the copper during the electroless deposition bath. The results also showed that the deposited layer on the metallized cBN particles was composed mainly of metallic copper. The produced 10 wt.% cBN/copper composite particles also underwent thermo-gravimetric analysis to investigate its stability at high temperature. It was revealed that the Ti-metallized cBN/copper composite powder has higher stability at 800 °C under the environmental conditions than the tin/silver-metallized and the un-metallized cBN/copper composite particles, respectively.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The corrosion of metallic surfaces poses significant challenges across industries such as petroleum, energy, and biomedical sectors, leading to structural degradation, safety risks, and substantial maintenance costs. Traditional organic and metallic coatings provide some protection, but their limited durability and susceptibility to harsh environmental conditions necessitate the development of more advanced and efficient solutions. This has driven significant interest in two-dimensional materials, with graphene being extensively studied for its exceptional mechanical strength and impermeability to gases and ions. However, while graphene offers short-term corrosion protection, its high electrical conductivity presents a long-term issue by promoting galvanic corrosion on metal surfaces. In contrast, hexagonal boron nitride (<jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN) has emerged as a promising alternative for anticorrosion coatings. <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN combines exceptional chemical stability, impermeability, and electrical insulation, making it particularly suited for long-term protection in highly corrosive or high-temperature environments. While <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN holds promise as anticorrosion material, challenges such as structural defects, agglomeration of nanosheets, and poor dispersion within coatings limit its performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of recent advancements in addressing these challenges, including novel functionalization strategies, scalable synthesis methods, and hybrid systems that integrate <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN with complementary materials. By bridging the gap between fundamental research and industrial applications, this review outlines the potential for <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN to revolutionize anticorrosion technologies. These obstacles necessitate advanced strategies such as surface functionalization to improve compatibility with polymer matrices and dispersion optimization to minimize agglomeration. Recent advancements highlight the incorporation of <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN into composite materials, which have shown significant advances in durability, adhesion, and overall performance. Future directions for <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN research emphasize scalable fabrication techniques to produce large-area, defect-free coatings suitable for industrial deployment. Furthermore, hybrid systems that integrate <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN with complementary materials are proposed to enhance corrosion resistance and address specific environmental and operational demands. These approaches hold the potential to establish <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-BN as a transformative material for next-generation anticorrosion technologies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Two-dimensional material (2DM) coatings exhibit complex and controversial interactions with biological matter, having shown in different contexts to induce bacterial cell death and contribute to mammalian cell growth and proliferation in vitro and tissue differentiation in vivo. Although several reports indicate that the morphologic and electronic properties of the coating, as well as its surface features (e.g., crystallinity, wettability, and chemistry), play a key role in the biological interaction, these kinds of interactions have not been fully understood yet. In this review, we report and classify the cellular interaction mechanisms observed in graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) coatings. Graphene and hBN were chosen as study materials to gauge the effect of two atomic-thick coatings with analogous lattice structure yet dissimilar electrical properties upon contact with living matter, allowing to discern among the observed effects and link them to specific material properties. In our analysis, we also considered the influence of crystallinity and surface roughness, detailing the mechanisms of interaction that make specific coatings of these 2DMs either hostile toward bacterial cells or innocuous for mammalian cells. In doing this, we discriminate among the material and surface properties, which are often strictly connected to the 2DM production technique, coating deposition and post-processing method. Building on this knowledge, the selection of 2DM coatings based on their specific characteristics will allow to engineer desired functionalities and devices. Antibacterial coatings to prevent biofouling, biocompatible platforms suitable for biomedical applications (e.g., wound healing, tissue repairing and regeneration, and novel biosensing devices) could be realized in the next future. Overall, a clear understanding on how the 2DM coating’s properties may modulate a specific bacterial or cellular response is crucial for any future innovation in the field.

Abstract:
Graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) (0, 1 wt% and 2 wt%) reinforced hydroxyapatite (HA), denoted by HA, HA-1G and HA-2G respectively, coatings were fabricated on titanium substrate (Ti-6Al-4V) through atmospheric plasma spraying. The major parameters such as porosity, crystallinity, mechanical properties, toughness and cell proliferation were manipulated by varying plasma power from 15 kW to 35 kW and content of GNPs. For the coating synthesized at all plasma power, GNPs were found to be retained by Raman spectroscopy. GNPs reinforcement has led to an improvement in the crystallinity of the composite coatings as compared to HA coatings. On the contrary to it, increase in plasma power from 15 kW to 35 kW resulted in decrease in crystallinity for all three individual coating. Further, Increment in plasma power from 15 kW to 35 kW delivered a significant enhancement in hardness, elastic modulus and fracture toughness up to 81%, 149% and 282% respectively for HA-1 wt% GNPs coating, while it improved to 20%, 50% and 173% respectively on the addition of 2 wt% GNPs in HA coating fabricated at 35 kW. Enhancement in hardness, elastic modulus and fracture toughness was due to three simultaneous reasons: (1) Reduction in porosity (2) Uniform dispersion of GNPs and (3) Toughening mechanism offered by GNPs. Further, the addition of GNPs showed a remarkable improvement in the rate of cell proliferation in the HA coating. A detailed discussion over the reasons behind every results have been made profoundly.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Architected material design enables cementitious materials to achieve highly desirable mechanical and functional performance for next-generation infrastructure. However, current architected cementitious materials require complex and energy-intensive fabrication, limiting their scalability and large-scale implementation. Inspired by the preparation of puff pastry, we propose a lamellar cementitious architected material fabricated by a simple rolling-folding process under ambient conditions. This material features a highly ordered lamellar architecture, consisting of alternating parallel cement lamellae and discrete plate-like cavities. This structure enables ductile fracture behavior, high fracture toughness, and effective thermal insulation. The specific fracture toughness of this material reaches up to 91 MPa·mm
                    <jats:sup>0.5</jats:sup>
                    /g·cm
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    , approximately 20 times higher than that of the cast counterpart, surpassing conventional reinforced cementitious composites and approaching the level of certain polymers. Meanwhile, its thermal conductivity decreases to 0.38 W/m·K, representing a 68.3% reduction relative to the cast counterpart, and outperforming lightweight cementitious materials with comparable densities. Furthermore, this material demonstrates good manufacturing efficiency, scalability, and geometric adaptability, overcoming the application limitations of existing architected cementitious materials. This study can help advance the development of next-generation infrastructure materials.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Colloidal based films have been widely developed for a wide range of applications including chemical and electrical barrier coatings, photonic materials, biomaterials, and pharmaceutical oral drug delivery. Many previous studies investigate methods to generate uniformity or desired stratification of the final components with a desired microstructure. Few studies have been able to investigate this microstructure in - situ during drying. This experimental study directly tracks fluorescent colloids that are either stable in suspension or have attractive interactions during the drying process using high speed laser scanning confocal microscopy to obtain details of microstructural evolution during drying. The colloidal microstructure in stable suspensions evolves continuously during drying. Microstructures in these systems have a signature Voronoi polyhedra distribution that is defined by lognormal curve having a constant standard deviation that only depends on its chemical composition. Those formulations having strongly attractive constituents have microstructure that is heterogeneous and non-monotonic due to the mechanics associated with internal convection and capillary forces. Toward the end of drying, the influence of the mode of microstructure rearrangements remains evident.

Abstract:
Abstract This research is motivated by the desire to control the solids distribution during the drying of a film containing particles of two different sizes. A variety of particle arrangements in dried films has been seen experimentally, including a thin layer of small particles at the top surface. However, it is not fully understood why this would occur. This work formulates and solves a colloidal hydrodynamics model for (i) diffusion alone and (ii) diffusion plus excluded volume diffusiophoresis, to determine their relative importance in affecting the particle arrangement. The methodology followed is to derive partial differential equations (PDEs) describing the motion of two components in a drying film. The diffusive fluxes are predicted by generalising the Stokes–Einstein diffusion coefficient, with the dispersion compressibility used to produce equations valid up until close packing. A further set of novel equations incorporating diffusiophoresis is derived. The diffusiophoretic mechanism investigated in this work is the small particles being excluded from a volume around the large particles. The resulting PDEs are scaled and solved numerically using a finite volume method. The model includes the chemical potentials of the particles, allowing for incorporation of any interaction term. The relative magnitudes of the fluxes of the differently sized particles are compared using scaling arguments and via numerical results. The diffusion results, without any inter-particle interactions, predict stratification of large particles to the top surface. Addition of excluded volume diffusiophoresis introduces a downwards flux on the large particles, that can result in small-on-top stratification, thus providing a potential explanation of the experimental observations.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Graphene nanoplatelet (GNP)-reinforced metal matrix composites (MMCs) represent a groundbreaking group of lightweight structural materials, offering exceptional combinations of strength, toughness, and multifunctionality that are critical for next-generation applications. Graphene imparts exceptional properties that significantly enhance the performance of lightweight alloys such as aluminum and magnesium. The review first examines the
                    <jats:italic>ex situ</jats:italic>
                    incorporation of GNPs into metal matrices and their effects on alloy solidification and mechanical properties based on process parameters, volume fraction, and matrix material. It then highlights two emerging
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    strategies, including the Covetic process, which employs electrically assisted processing (EAP) to synthesize graphene within metallic melts, and CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    bubbling in magnesium alloys to form carbon–metal (C–M) bonds. Particular emphasis is placed on mechanisms of C–M bonding, dispersion challenges, and interfacial bonding between the metallic matrices and graphene. This review emphasizes the potential of graphene-reinforced MMCs across industries and identifies the persistent barriers to process upscaling.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p><p>Magnesium is a lightweight metal with a high strength-to-weight ratio, making it an ideal material for improving fuel efficiency. However, its poor mechanical properties necessitate the need for researchers to find ways of improving them for this material to find wider acceptance in industry. This study examines the grain refinement capabilities of an aluminum-carbon (graphite) composite in cast AZ91E magnesium alloy. With increasing carbon addition, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and ductility improved, while yield strength (YS) remained largely unchanged. The fracture mechanism also remained unchanged with increasing carbon addition, showing mixed-mode fracture in samples of highest and lowest ductility. The nucleation mechanism was determined to be duplex nucleation of Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub> and Al<sub>8</sub>Mn<sub>5</sub>. X-ray diffraction analysis confirmed that the Al-C inoculant contained Al4C3 after sintering; however, most Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub> was formed in-situ during the melting and casting process.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Hybrid aluminum matrix composites (HAMCs) reinforced with graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) and secondary reinforcements have emerged as promising lightweight structural materials due to their superior strength, wear resistance, and multifunctional performance. This review critically evaluates recent developments in GNPs-reinforced HAMCs, categorizing them into carbide-assisted, oxide-assisted, carbonaceous, and emerging sustainable hybrid systems. The influence of processing routes including semi-solid stir casting (compocasting), ultrasonic-assisted stir casting (UASC), powder metallurgy (PM), friction stir processing (FSP), accumulative roll bonding (ARB), and laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) on reinforcement dispersion, interfacial bonding, and resultant properties (grain refinement, load-transfer mechanisms, etc.) is systematically discussed. Further, particular emphasis is placed on the role of the hybrid reinforcements in improving the mechanical and tribological performances of the HAMCs in reference to their processing techniques. Comparative analysis reveals that carbide-assisted systems provide the highest strengthening response, where Al/(GNPs+SiC) composites achieve tensile strengths up to 589 MPa through severe grain refinement, while GNPs+WC systems exhibit nearly 350% relative strength enhancement. Among oxide-assisted systems, L-PBF fabricated AA2024/(0.2GNPs+1ZrO2) (wt.%) composites attain a peak tensile strength of 624 MPa after T6 treatment due to the formation of a crack-free bimodal microstructure. Carbonaceous hybrids such as reduced graphene oxide (rGO)+CNTs systems demonstrate an excellent balance between strength (460 MPa) and ductility (31.6%) through interconnected carbon networks that suppress crack propagation. Tribologically, graphene-based tribo-films significantly reduce friction and wear, with GO+CNTs hybrids achieving a minimum coefficient of friction of 0.295, whereas GNPs+B4C and GNPs+waste-derived Al hybrid systems exhibit excellent wear resistance with wear rates as low as 1.9x10-3 mm3 m-1. The review further highlights key challenges including reinforcement agglomeration, porosity, and interfacial instability at higher GNPs loadings (>1–2 wt.%). Overall, the study provides a comparative and data-driven framework for designing next-generation HAMCs for aerospace, automotive, defense, and thermal-management applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract Graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of sp2 hybridized carbon atoms densely packed within a hexagonal crystal lattice, owes a significant portion of its rapidly expanding usage in various fields of industry and science to its large surface area, lightweight, unique electronic and thermal properties, and extraordinary mechanical properties that it possesses. Using lightweight and high-strength materials leads to a substantial decrease in fuel consumption as well as an increase in payload. Among the numerous candidates to fulfill the aforementioned requirements, Al alloys and specifically, Al matrix composites (AMCs) reinforced with various graphene particles (nano-sheets, nano-platelets, etc.) stand out owing to their inherent lightweight, high specific strength and modulus, superior ductility and excellent thermal conductivity. In this paper, it has been endeavored to provide a comprehensive overview of the various methods of the synthesis and fabrication of graphene-reinforced AMCs with an overall intention of achieving a homogeneous distribution of graphene within the Al matrix. The emphasis of this review has been largely placed upon the detailed examination of the mechanical properties of these composites described in the recent literature published in this field. The strengthening mechanisms of Al/graphene composites, as well as the parameters affecting the strength and ductility achieved by graphene, such as the agglomeration of graphene within the Al matrix and Al/graphene interfacial reactions, have been elucidated. The role of graphene on the electrical and thermal properties of graphene-reinforced AMCs and the directions for future research are addressed. It should be noted, however, that while a diligent analysis of various works published in the field of Al/graphene composites has been carried out in this review, an exact comparison between the varying stages of each work, or their final properties is impractical, mainly due to the differences in the used initial substances, processing, and analyses.

Abstract:
Based on a critical analysis of the current state and prospects of development of the problem of pyrometallurgical recovery/extraction of aluminum from aluminum-bearing industrial waste, the need to replace traditional, electrocarbonothermic processes and melting process units with innovative, plasma carbothermal processes and furnace-reactors, with the possibility of reverse feeding and recovery of gasified during melting metal and metal oxide components is substantiated. On the basis of this analysis a new technological scheme of smelting with a new design of plasma-arc furnace-reactor, which provides a solution to the problem using a special hollow double-shell graphite cathode connected to the system of circulating supply of gases separated from the reaction zone, was developed and presented. The proposed technological scheme also differs in the use of such highly active liquid and gaseous reagents as carbon-containing reducing agents as calcium carbide (CaC2) and methane (CH4). The main features of chemism of reducing processes are described. It is shown that by replacing traditional coke with anodized calcium carbide and natural gas (methane) the recovery rate of aluminum oxide (Al 29-34%) and silica (SiO2) and hematite (Fe2O3) present with it increases to 80-99%. Specific power consumption is reduced by 35-40%, the 90-95% reduction in the loss of target elements, the 80% reduction in the emission of greenhouse carbon dioxide, which is replaced by a very valuable recyclable synthesis gas - CO-H2. By additionally feeding separate portions of quartzite and steel-rolling scale in the furnace-reactor, a complex alloy-ligature of Fe-Si-Al-Ca system is melted, with the ratio of components: 1:[1.3-2]:[1.3-1.2]:[0.9-1.25]. With the introduction into industrial practice of the plasma carbothermal process of aluminum reduction from secondary aluminum dumping slags accumulated in the world (4 million tons/year), it will be possible to return up to 1-1.5 million tons/year of aluminum to the production processing cycle.

Abstract:
Boron-based nano-formulations look very promising for biomedical applications, including photo- and boron neutron capture therapies, but the fabrication of non-toxic water-dispersible boron nanoparticles (NPs), which contain the highest boron atom concentration, is difficult using currently available chemical and plasma synthesis methods. Here, we demonstrate purely aqueous synthesis of clean boron NPs by methods of femtosecond laser ablation from a solid boron target in water, thus free of any toxic organic solvents, and characterize their properties. We show that despite highly oxidizing water ambience, the laser-ablative synthesis process follows an unusual scenario leading to the formation of boron NPs together with boric acid (H3BO3) as an oxidation by-product coating the nanoparticles, which acts to stabilize the elemental boron NPs dispersion. We then demonstrate the purification of boron NPs from residual boric acid in deionized water, followed by their coating with polyethylene glycol to improve colloidal stability and biocompatibility. It was found that the formed NPs have a spherical shape with averaged size of about 37 nm, and are composed of elemental boron in mostly amorphous phase with the presence of certain crystalline fraction. The synthesized NPs demonstrate low toxicity and exhibit strong absorption in the NIR window of relative tissue transparency, promising their use in photoacoustic imaging and phototherapy, in addition to their promise for neutron capture therapy. This combined potential ability of generating imaging and therapy functionalities makes laser-synthesized B NPs a very promising multifunctional agent for biomedical applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The widely used high-density polyethylene (HDPE) polymer has inadequate mechanical and thermal properties for structural applications. To overcome this challenge, nano zinc oxide (ZnO) and nano boron oxide (B2O3) doped lignin-containing cellulose nanocrystals (L-CNC) were blended in the polymer matrix. The working hypothesis is that lignin will prevent CNC aggregation, and metal oxides will reduce the flammability of polymers by modifying their degradation pathways. This research prepared and incorporated safe, effective, and eco-friendly hybrid systems of nano ZnO/L-CNC and nano B2O3/L-CNC into the HDPE matrix to improve their physio-mechanical and fire-retardant properties. The composites were characterized using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, thermo-gravimetric analysis, differential scanning calorimetry, dynamic mechanical analysis, horizontal burning test, and microcalorimetry test. The results demonstrated a substantial increase in mechanical properties and a reduction in flammability. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) images showed some agglomeration and irregular distribution of the inorganic oxides.</jats:p>

Its mechanistic discussion states that drying-induced evaporation and capillary action generate tensile stress, with capillary pressure arising from surface tension and meniscus curvature between particles. The excerpt presents the Griffith energy-balance framework: total energy is the sum of mechanical and surface contributions, U = UM + US = UE + UL + US, and equilibrium at crack extension satisfies dU/dl = 0. For constant loading, the mechanical energy decreases as a crack advances while surface energy increases. The excerpt provides only partial information relevant to critical cracking thickness and does not state a specific critical thickness or its dependence on particle size, surface tension, or substrate constraint. It reports that the critical cracking stress follows the Griffith-derived scaling σc ∼ (G/h²)^(1/3), with G representing the shear modulus and h the film thickness at cracking. For polymer–particle coatings, G is replaced by an effective modulus Ge. The associated stress-growth argument predicts that nucleation is reduced in thicker films and at higher particle loadings. ## pqac-00000005

From text 'manousis2026castingselfreflectionthreedimensional pages 159-166'.

J Manousis. Casting self-reflection: three-dimensional mirrors within kiln-cast glass sculpture. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt provides experimental observations about ZYP Coatings’ boron-nitride products, but it does not include manufacturer statements from ZYP, Momentive, Saint-Gobain Combat, or Henze HeBoCoat concerning aerosol-spray coating thickness, recoating over existing layers, or stripping/removing a coat before recoating. For ZYP paste applications, the researchers applied three layers, diluted each with 15% deionised water by weight, and pre-wetted the refractory surface with two or three coats of water to promote even coverage. The results indicate that excessive coating thickness is associated with cracking or crazing during firing: two hand-applied coats produced edge cracking in some Bullseye tests, while three coats caused full-surface cracking. Thick BNZS applications also left visible impressions on the glass. By contrast, compressed-air spray application—using coatings diluted by 10% deionised water, described as the maximum dilution advised by ZYP—produced no observed sticking or cracking. The excerpt also states that ZYP coatings can flake or lose performance when exposed to excess heat and water, especially in lost-wax casting, but it gives no specific strip-before-recoat procedure or guidance on applying aerosol coats over existing coats.

Christopher Fleming. Oxidation‐led decomposition of hexagonal boron nitride coatings on alloy substrates at 900 °c: chromia‐formers. Materials and Corrosion, 70:853-867, Jan 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/maco.201810532, doi:10.1002/maco.201810532. This article has 2 citations.

At high temperature, hexagonal boron nitride oxidizes from approximately 800°C, producing molten boron trioxide (B2O3) and gaseous nitrogen; alternative pathways can produce nitric oxide or nitrogen dioxide instead. The principal stoichiometric reaction given is BN + 3/4 O2 → 1/2 B2O3 + 1/2 N2. At 900°C, B2O3 is above its approximately 450°C melting point and forms a molten, tacky phase that can encapsulate BN particles and increasingly limit diffusion, causing oxidation of BN powder to level off. B2O3 is hygroscopic and can absorb atmospheric moisture. In wet air, it may react with water vapor to form volatile metaboric acid (HBO2) and orthoboric acid (H3BO3). The cited studies disagree in the extent of acid formation: one detected little metaboric acid below 1000°C, while another detected metaboric acid and trace orthoboric acid at 700°C. In experiments between 800 and 1100°C, wet air caused an initial mass gain followed by linear mass loss, attributed to a balance between BN oxidation and volatilization. The supplied excerpt does not specifically describe the subsequent behavior of a fired BN coating during ordinary humid exposure, so coating-specific conclusions cannot be established from these pages alone.

The excerpt indicates that when molten aluminum contacts carbonaceous material such as graphite or graphene, Al4C3 formation is thermodynamically favored because carbon has very low solubility in aluminum and the carbide reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy (-196 kJ/mol at 298 K). In aluminum-containing systems, including an Al-bearing copper alloy, contact with graphite can therefore promote interfacial aluminum–carbon reactions, particularly at elevated temperature and with sufficient process time. The cited aluminum–carbon phase-diagram discussion states that Al4C3 is thermodynamically favorable below 2100 °C; this does not mean that 2100 °C is a required formation temperature. Rather, carbide may form throughout relevant molten-metal processing temperatures, depending on kinetics, exposure time, carbon surface condition, and local chemistry. Metallurgically, formation is undesirable: carbide can grow from the aluminum/carbon interface toward the carbon reinforcement, consume or damage the interface, reduce load-transfer capability, and initiate microcracks because Al4C3 is brittle. Excessive carbide formation therefore degrades mechanical performance and complicates casting or melt processing. The excerpt also notes that conventional ex situ liquid routes cannot reliably incorporate carbon into aluminum without possible carbide formation, motivating alternative methods intended to prevent or limit carbide formation.

Wetting behaviour

One of the most well-known properties of boron nitride is its poor wettability against many
metal melts. These include among others melts of aluminium and magnesium. The wetting of
ceramic material by a melt is usually described by the wetting angle 0 which is determined by
using a heating microscope according to the method of the sessile drop. Here, the contact angle
0 of a melt drop is measured on the substrate (see Figure 6). Large angles (>90°) mean a poor
wettability according to the drawn example, small angles (<90°C) in contrasts represent a good
 wettability.

          describe their wetting behaviour.



                                          167Figure 7 shows the contact angles of molten aluminium in contact with boron nitride, silicon
nitride and alumina in dependence of the temperature (6). Up to 900°C boron nitride is only
poorly wetted by aluminium and shows contact angles of 160°C. Between 900  ... 1000°C the
contact angle value decreases, but is well above those of A^Os and SisN^ However, in the
temperature range which is interesting to aluminium casters, the wetting behaviour of boron
nitride is far superior to oxide ceramics like alumina and even a little better than other nitrides
like silicon nitride. Thus boron nitride  is an ideal release agent  for casting and shaping
processes in light metal casthouses and foundries.
