Composition of coatings based on boron nitride

Various types of boron nitride coatings are available on the market. They differ in types of
boron nitride used for the production of such coatings, in carrier liquids preferred as well as in
the solid content and refractory binder.

Boron nitride

Boron nitride are commercially available with BN concentrations between 95 and 98 mass-%
 for refractory and common casting applications. If higher BN concentrations are required, e. g.
 for laboratory and research applications, BN concentrations >98.5 mass-%. The balance will be
 mainl

 Carrier liquids

 The choice of carrier liquids is mainly governed by technological aspects, but other points of
 view such as environmental and safety concerns must also taken into account. Water is an
 inexpensive, readily available and non-hazardous option. However, forced drying of applied
 coatings will be necessary in most cases. Alternatively organic solvents such as alcohols
 (ethanol, 2-propanol) may be used, but these formulations have to be labelled according to
 hazardous materials regulations.

                                          168Refractory binder

Boron nitride coatings can be produced without any refractory binder; the adherence of the
particles can be achieved with their surface energy alone. Specific surface areas of at least
25m2/g are necessary for this. Most applications, however, require a coating with reasonable
adherence which makes the use of refractory binders necessary. For coating ceramic substrates
with low thermal expansion, phosphate-containing binders have proven to be well suited. These
binders harden when heated to 800 ... 900°C and result in a strong yet brittle bond. They cannot
be used for high-thermal-expansion substrates like metals. Here binders on the basis of A^Os
for higher temperatures (>1000°C) or AkOs-SiC^ for temperatures below 1000°C can be used.
If the coating is meant to remain soft throughout the whole temperature range, clay minerals
may be the binder of choice.

Application of coatings based on boron nitride

In order to use boron nitride in casthouses and foundries it is necessary to apply in the form of
coatings. In most cases these coatings are water-based suspensions like house paint. These
boron-nitride-coatings are applied like ordinary house paints by brushing or dipping. If  it is
required to coat small objects, dipping can be an application method of choice as well. Spraying
is also possible and is recommended for coating larger surfaces and for hot objects which are
difficult to paint. For spraying, a blow cup or a spray gun operated by pressurized air can be
used. Nozzle sizes of 1.5mm will give best results.

Application to DC casting systems

The most commonly used application of Boron-Nitride-Coating in the DC casting process is the
coating of mould transition plates. A coat of boron-nitride-coating ensures the non-wetting of
the melt during casting and the release of remains of aluminium during the casting breaks,
boron-nitride-coating  is applied to the ceramic  transition plate by brushing or  spraying.
However, with the application it is important not to coat the porous graphite ring, because this
would interrupt the gas flow through the mould.

Another similar application of boron-nitride-coating is the coating of the thimbles, usually
made of fused  silica, boron-nitride-coating is applied by brushing or spraying on the inner
surface. This enables the operator to easily remove the remaining metal during the casting
breaks. The coating is applied before the casting table is put into service for the first time and
between casting breaks when the remaining metal is removed.

The third application to DC machines is the coating of the refractory lining of the distribution
trough. In contrast to the application to transition plates and thimbles discussed before, this
application is done by spraying. However, the first coat can be done by brushing. The spraying
is done during each casting break, when the trough is tilted and the casting pit emptied. The
boron nitride ensures an easy and quick removal of the remaining aluminium. The boron-
nitride-coating makes cleaning of the trough easier and is well accepted by the working force.

## 2. rudolph2013boronnitriderelease pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000027)

          BORON NITRIDE RELEASE COATINGS

                             Stephan Rudolph
                    Euro fur angewandte Mineraloge
                              Tonisvorst, Germany

                                      Abstract

Boron  nitride  is an advanced  ceramic  material with outstanding chemical and thermal
properties. It is often called "white graphite" because  it has a graphite-like structure, but in
contrast to graphite, it is white. It is an excellent high-temperature solid lubricant, is stable at
high temperature and - most important for casting and foundry applications - is not wetted by
many metallic melts like aluminium, magnesium and zinc.

In order to be able to use the advantages of boron nitride in casthouse and foundry applications,
we developed coatings on the basis of boron nitride particularly for the application within
casting shops. These coatings are applied like ordinary house paints by brushing or using a
spray gun. They are perfect release agents used in aluminium foundries for the protection of
ladles,  dies ingot mould, permanent moulds thermocouples and ceramic  structures. These
coatings provide an excellent non- sticking and lubricating surface to which neither aluminium
nor magnesium will adhere.

Boron nitride coatings are also proven release agents for coating thimbles, transition plates and
refractory linings of distribution troughs of DC casting machines. During casting breaks, these
coatings ensure the perfect and easy release of remaining aluminium without damaging the
refractory substrate.

Boron nitride release coatings are available as water-based paints as concentrates as well as
ready-to-use formulations. For an easier application in suitable environments, these coatings are
available in aerosol cans too.

In contrast to graphite coatings and other (red mud) readily-used coatings boron nitride release
coatings are stable in air (up to 1000°C), show excellent non-wetting behaviour (the best in the
field of ceramics) and very good lubrication properties even at high temperatures. These very
advanced characteristics make boron nitride release coatings a product of the first choice to
foundrymen.





                                                    7th Australian Asian Pacific Conference
                                   Aluminium Cast House Technology
                                               Edited by P.R. Whiteley
                       IMS (The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society), 2001


                                          163Introduction

Release coatings are used in DC casting, ingot casting, sand casting and with different die
casting processes. Beyond that they are used as a surface protection for ladles, troughs, launders
and various other equipment which come into contact with metallic melts. They have the
function

- to prevent a reaction of the melt with the mould material,
- to influence the heat transfer locally between melt and shaping surface,
- to enable a separation between casting and the mould when discharging the mould.

Beyond that coatings may react neither with the melt nor with the mould material. The coating
should be able to be applied with an even layer thickness on the shaping surfaces, should not
adhere at the surface of the cast parts partially and, if they are applied on as wear-coating, they
should not build up.

Beyond that release coatings should be environmentally  friendly. The characteristics  like
chemical and thermal stability, thermal conductivity and separation efficiency, necessary for
the  fulfilment  of these  functions, depend primarily on the  refractory  fillers used  in the
respective coatings.

Beside the classical refractory fillers such as graphite, zircon or talc also the use of advanced
ceramic materials  is considered. Here above  all boron nitride  is to be mentioned, which
indicates a number of interesting characteristics, which make the use as a refractory  filler in
release coatings to appear meaningful (1,2).

Physical and chemical characteristics of boron nitride and comparison with graphite

Boron nitride occurs in two modifications. The cubic high pressure modification however is
ignored in the following paper and only the hexagonal modification is regarded. In the literature
the hexagonal boron nitride is often called "white graphite", since  it shows a structure very
similar  to  that  of  graphite.  Therefore   it  appears meaningful  to  compare  the  physical
characteristics of boron nitride with those of graphite. Some important physical characteristics
are shown in Table I.

                                          164 Crystal structure

 Both boron nitride and graphite crystallize in a hexagonal layer lattice with a very similar layer
 distance (see Figure 1) (3,  4). While for boron nitride a layer distance of 666.1pm was
 measured, graphite shows a value of 669,6pm. Additionally both materials show similar

 This is due to the plate-like formation of both materials. The layers of the lattice may be shifted
 easily, therefore both graphite as well as boron nitride are suitable as solid lubricants. A
 scanning electron micrograph (Figure 2) shows the plate-like particles of boron nitride powder
used as a starting material for boron nitride coatings

Thermal stability

However large differences can be observed to thermal stability and oxidation resistance of
boron nitride and graphite. Both materials show a very high point of sublimation which is
clearly situated above that of other ceramic materials. In Figure 3 the melting points or points

sublimation of 3650°C. Boron nitride with a sublimation point of almost 3000°C is in second
place. This is clearly above other ceramic materials such as SisN^ SiC or A^Os or even ZrOi.
However,  the  application  temperature  of  all  ceramic  materials  is  well  below  these

The third application to DC machines is the coating of the refractory lining of the distribution
trough. In contrast to the application to transition plates and thimbles discussed before, this
application is done by spraying. However, the first coat can be done by brushing. The spraying
is done during each casting break, when the trough is tilted and the casting pit emptied. The

The recoat is done after each casting. However, in contrast to terracote red mud coatings and

Casting of ingots

Boron-nitride-coatings find  its application in the area of the secondary metal producers and
recycling firms, too. With this application the ingot moulds are coated in order to ensure for the
                                          169perfect release and high quality surfaces of their ingots. The boron-nitride-coatings can be used
for casting aluminium and magnesium as well as for zinc and lead. When casting magnesium
with boron-nitride-coatings it will be noticed that the formation of oxides of the surface of the
ingots is suppressed. This makes recycling of magnesium easier because the oxides cannot be
removed from the melt because of their density being in the same order of magnitude of the
molten metal.

Die casting / gravity die casting

It is generally known to use boron-nitride-coatings for the coating of dies in gravity die casting
and low pressure die casting processes. The very good high temperature lubricating and release
properties ensure the perfect release of the casting from the mould. The boron-nitride-coating
dramatically reduces the sticking of the casting to the mould. The boron-nitride-coating also
suppresses or reduces the distortion of the casting, especially during the unloading of low
pressure die moulds.

Summary

Boron-nitride-coatings have an excellent thermal and chemical stability in the temperature
range that is of interest to aluminium casters. It does not react with the metal melt or the
refractory nor does it disintegrate. Boron nitride shows a very good non-wetting behaviour, one
of the best known in the fields of ceramics. Boron nitride is an excellent high-temperature
lubricant; therefore  it is an excellent lubrication and parting agent when unloading castings
from the moulds or removing remains of aluminium from the casting machines. Boron nitride is
of white colour. Therefore, in contrast to graphite,  it is a good way to keep the casthouse /
foundry cleaner.

 2                      processing of Li-ion battery electrodes


 3


 4         Kelsey Rollag1, Daniel Juarez-Robles2, [name redacted]3, [name redacted]3, Partha P. Mukherjee2


 5         1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA

13                              Journal of the Electrochemical Society


14                                              or


15                         ACS Applied Energy Materials

                                            120                                         Abstract

21   Unlike conventional electrode processing for Li-ion batteries, which use the expensive and highly

22    toxic organic solvent, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), aqueous processing simply employs

23   deionized water as the solvent in electrode preparation. However, thick aqueous processed

24   cathodes have been found to crack as they dry. In this study, the influence of electrode drying

25   temperature and thickness on cracking was investigated. LiNi1/3Mn1/3Co1/3O2 cathodes prepared

26   with a novel hydrophilic binder, modified styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), were coated at various

27    thicknesses and dried at temperatures ranging from 20 °C to 70 °C. Experiments revealed cracking

28   worsens with increased electrode thickness, as well as elevated drying temperatures. No evidence

29    of cracking during the evaporation phase was found. However, cracks were formed during the

30    capillary driven phase. Images of electrode surfaces were processed to quantify crack dimensions

31   and crack intensity factor (CIF). Average crack length and width, as well as CIF, increased with

32   drying temperature and electrode thickness. In addition, half cells were constructed and cycled at

33   a C-rate of C/20 to study the electrochemical performance of the thick electrodes. It was found

34    that increasing crack density correlated with a decline in discharge capacity due to the high charge

35    transfer resistance of cracked, thick electrodes.





                                            236   Introduction

37   Widespread use of electric vehicles hinges on the advancement of energy storage technologies

38   such as lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Current research and development endeavors are focused on

39    increasing the energy density of a battery while simultaneously reducing manufacturing costs [1].

40   Energy density can be improved, and cost can be reduced by optimizing the number of inactive

41   components in a cell with the implementation of thicker electrodes. Furthermore, cost can be

42    significantly reduced with aqueous electrode processing [2].

43   To meet high energy density demands, thick positive electrodes of 100~200 μm are required in

44   LIBs. However, when a thick cathode is prepared via aqueous processing, the electrode coating

45    cracks as it dries. Du et al. showed that the severity of such crack formations progressively worsens

46    for increasingly thick electrodes [3], as shown in Figure 1.


47   The electrode with 15.0 mg/cm2 areal loading exhibited only subtle microcracks. However, the

48    electrode with 17.5 mg/cm2 loading had pronounced cracks with an average width and length of

49   50 μm and 300 μm, respectively. Cracks are seen to propagate further and increase in number as

50    the mass loading was increased. In fact, the electrode with 25 mg/cm2 loading had cracks which

51   protruded all the way through to the aluminum foil current collector, resulting in weakened

52   adhesion and delamination of the electrode from the current collector.


53   Consequently, aqueous processed cathodes are restricted to conservative thicknesses to avoid

54    cracking. A standard aqueous processed positive electrode with areal loading of ~12.5 mg/cm2 is

55   completely devoid of cracks. Cracks appear when electrode areal mass loadings exceed ~15

56   mg/cm2.





                                            357   Drying-induced cracks have been widely studied in concrete [4, 5], desiccated soils [6, 7], ceramic

58    films [8, 9], colloidal dispersions [10, 11], and latex films [12, 13]. There is a general consensus

59    that capillary pressure induced stresses are the cause of cracking in drying particulate dispersions

60    [13-16]. Initially, particles suspended in a solvent are coated on a rigid substrate. Evaporation

61    drives the air-liquid interface towards the substrate. When the air-liquid interface encounters the

62   subsequently close-packed particle network, capillary action forms liquid menisci among surface

63    particles, giving rise to a negative capillary pressure.


64    Scaling inversely with pore radius, capillary pressure can be enormous. The pressure gradient

65    across the air-liquid interface puts the entire film into compression, shrinking the film as it dries.

66   Film shrinkage is constrained by the rigid substrate and stress is generated in the film. If this stress

67   exceeds a critical value, the film will crack to alleviate it. Tirumkudulu and Russel [13] derived an

68    expression for the critical stress required for the initiation of a single crack in a thin film:

Abstract:
Copper-based materials have long been used for their outstanding thermal and electrical conductivities in various applications, such as heat exchangers, induction heat coils, cooling channels, radiators, and electronic connectors. The development of advanced copper alloys has broadened their utilization to include structural applications in harsh service conditions found in industries like oil and gas, marine, power plants, and water treatment, where good corrosion resistance and a combination of high strength, wear, and fatigue tolerance are critical. These advanced multi-component structures often have complex designs and intricate geometries, requiring extensive metallurgical processing routes and the joining of the individual components into a final structure. Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized the way complex structures are designed and manufactured. It has reduced the processing steps, assemblies, and tooling while also eliminating the need for joining processes. However, the high thermal conductivity of copper and its high reflectivity to near-infrared radiation present challenges in the production of copper alloys using fusion-based AM processes, especially with Yb-fiber laser-based techniques. To overcome these difficulties, various solutions have been proposed, such as the use of high-power, low-wavelength laser sources, preheating the build chamber, employing low thermal conductivity building platforms, and adding alloying elements or composite particles to the feedstock material. This article systematically reviews different aspects of AM processing of common industrial copper alloys and composites, including copper-chrome, copper-nickel, tin-bronze, nickel-aluminum bronze, copper-carbon composites, copper-ceramic composites, and copper-metal composites. It focuses on the state-of-the-art AM techniques employed for processing different copper-based materials and the associated technological and metallurgical challenges, optimized processing variables, the impact of post-printing heat treatments, the resulting microstructural features, physical properties, mechanical performance, and corrosion response of the AM-fabricated parts. Where applicable, a comprehensive comparison of the results with those of their conventionally fabricated counterparts is provided.

Abstract:
This paper studies the influence of B2O3 on the structure, properties and antibacterial abilities of sol-gel-derived TiO2/TeO2/B2O3 powders. Titanium(IV) butoxide, telluric(VI) acid and boric acid were used as precursors. Differences were observed in the degree of decomposition of Ti butoxide in the presence of H3BO3 and H6TeO6 acids. The phase transformations of the obtained gels in the temperature range of 200–700 °C were investigated by XRD. Composite materials containing an amorphous phase and different crystalline phases (metallic Te, α-TeO2, anatase, rutile and TiTe3O8) were prepared. Heating at 400 °C indicated a crystalline-to-amorphous-phase ratio of approximately 3:1. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis showed the preparation of plate-like TiO2 nanoparticles. The IR results showed that the short-range order of the amorphous phases that are part of the composite materials consists of TiO6, BO3, BO4 and TeO4 structural units. Free B2O3 was not detected in the investigated compositions which could be related to the better connectivity between the building units as compared to binary TiO2/B2O3 compositions. The UV-Vis spectra of the investigated gels exhibited a red shift of the cut-off due to the presence of boron and tellurium units. The binary sample achieved the maximum photodegradation efficiency (94%) toward Malachite green dye under UV irradiation, whereas the ternary sample photoactivity was very low. The compositions exhibited promising antibacterial activity against E. coli NBIMCC K12 407.

Abstract:
The present study is aimed at investigating the utilization of two crucial industrial wastes, borogypsum and silica fume, as the main raw materials in the production of building materials. For this aim, different receipts were designed from boron waste (borogypsum) belonging to Emet Boric Acid factory (Kütahya/Turkey) and silica fume, which was taken from Electrometallurgy facilities (Antalya/Turkey). Mixtures were prepared so that the amount of waste material used in the composition was 90%, and the remaining 10% was binder clay. The samples were prepared with different proportions of both wastes were pressed uniaxially at 10 MPa, and the shaped samples were then fired at 1000, 1050, 1100, and 1150 °C. Physical and mechanical tests, as well as mineralogical and microstructural analyses, were carried out on the fired samples. The technical properties of the samples derived from the wastes were evaluated depending on the type of waste material and its usage amounts, and firing temperatures. It has been understood that the use of high Borogypsum will cause high firing loss, which will negatively affect the dimensional stability of the material. Moreover, with silica fume addition to borogypsum, the water absorption and porosity values increased, and the strength values decreased accordingly. Consequently, the water absorption and bending strength values obtained in the samples prepared from a mixture of 70% borogypsum and 20% silica fume can be considered the usage as a wall tile is possible since they coincide with the technical properties defined in the EN ISO 10545-3 and EN ISO 10545-4 standards, respectively.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A new method of creating a multilayer scintillation element for the registration of thermal neutrons using 3D printing technology on an FDM printer has been developed. The influence of thermophysical parameters of printing materials on the geometric shape and functional properties of the printed product was investigated. Optimal settings of the printing technology were selected. Samples of the scintillation element, which consists of layers of light guides alternating with scintillator layers, have been produced. Polystyrene was used as the light guide. A composite material based on polystyrene with a filler of zinc sulfide powder activated by silver, with the addition of a boron oxide (B2O3) neutron converter – ZnS:Ag/B2O3 – was used as a scintillator. The use of 3D printing with two materials in a single technological cycle made it possible to significantly simplify the process of creating a scintillation element compared to traditional technologies. The thermal neutron registration efficiency of the scintillation element sample created using 3D printing technology is 68%, which is comparable to the modern analogs of solid-state detectors created using traditional technology.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal foams offer attractive properties for lightweight structures. This study presents the development of a powder metallurgical aluminum alloy intended for foamable wires that can be used in additive manufacturing processes such as wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Unlike established aluminum wrought alloys, whose melting range is not well suited for foaming, or cast alloys which are not easily extruded into thin wires, the custom AlMg2Si1.2 alloy developed in this study combines a melting interval matched to the decomposition of pre-oxidized blowing agent (TiH
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) with a low alloying content suitable for high extrusion ratios. For this, the alloy composition was determined using thermodynamic calculations. The material was then cast into billets, which were extruded into rod electrodes. Pre-alloyed metal powder was produced from these electrodes using electrode induction melting inert gas atomization (EIGA), and the influence of atomization gas parameters on powder properties was investigated. Increasing the gas pressure from 16.8 bar to 23.0 bar reduced the median particle size from 51 to 40 µm. The best flowability was observed for the fraction 63–90 µm. A solidus temperature of 560 °C and a liquidus of 646 °C were determined by differential scanning calorimetry, aligning with the principal hydrogen-release peak of the blowing agent. Foam samples produced from the powder confirmed the material’s foamability, reaching porosities of 64–68%, as determined by X-ray microscopy. These results indicate that AlMg2Si1.2 processed via EIGA yields reproducible, highly porous foams, and is a suitable basis for foamable wires in WAAM.
                  </jats:p>

## pqac-00000031

From text 'rollag2019dryingtemperatureand pages 1-6'.

Kelsey Rollag, Daniel Juarez-Robles, [name redacted], [name redacted], and Partha P. Mukherjee. Drying temperature and capillarity-driven crack formation in aqueous processing of li-ion battery electrodes. ACS Applied Energy Materials, 2:4464-4476, Jun 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.9b00704, doi:10.1021/acsaem.9b00704. This article has 97 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt presents the Singh–Tirumkudulu critical crack-free thickness model, hmax = 0.64[(G M φrcp R^3)/(2γ)]^(1/2)[2γ/(Pmax R)]^(3/2), where R is particle radius, γ is liquid–vapor surface tension, G is particle shear modulus, M is coordination number, and φrcp is the random-close-packing volume fraction. The dimensionless maximum capillary pressure is specified through Pmax R/(2γ) = (3 cosθ/2)[φrcp/(1−φrcp)]. Substitution shows that, with the other parameters fixed, hmax scales as R^(3/2) and γ^(−1/2): larger particles permit a thicker crack-free film, while lower solvent surface tension increases the allowable thickness. The excerpt explicitly states the γ and G dependencies but does not provide numerical values for hBN platelet modulus, coordination number, packing fraction, contact angle, or the acetone/ethanol mixture’s surface tension. Therefore, it supports scaling estimates for hBN radii of approximately 1–5 μm, but a numerical hmax requires those additional material and solvent parameters. If all other quantities are held constant, increasing R from 1 to 5 μm would increase hmax by 5^(3/2), approximately 11.2-fold.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'ghosh2023studyofdesiccation pages 148-153'.

A Ghosh. Study of desiccation crack patterns in aqueous clay suspensions and the role of charge distribution in formation of cracks under electric field. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt indicates that platelet-shaped clay particles strongly influence drying cracks through their anisotropic, layered packing rather than simply through particle size. Bentonite platelets create interparticle d-spaces, while much smaller Laponite® discs can act as nanofillers. At an approximately 1:1 Laponite:bentonite ratio, Laponite® fills the spaces between bentonite platelets and produces a compact, homogeneous layered or “house-of-card” structure. This improves shear-stress transmission during drying and almost completely suppresses desiccation fractures, even when film thickness is varied. When the ratio is bentonite-rich (about 1:3), unfilled gaps remain between platelets and become crack-nucleation sites. When Laponite® is excessive (about 3:1), it forms flocs on bentonite surfaces, which also nucleate cracks. Thus, platelet shape promotes directional packing, interlocking, and stress transfer, but it can also generate defects, voids, or aggregates that localize cracking if packing is incomplete. The excerpt does not discuss hBN or provide a direct comparison with spherical particles. In general, however, its clay results suggest that plate-like particles can form anisotropic layered networks with crack suppression at favorable packing conditions, whereas spherical particles would not provide the same platelet-to-platelet d-space filling and layered stress-transfer mechanism.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'ghosh2023studyofdesiccation pages 106-112'.

A Ghosh. Study of desiccation crack patterns in aqueous clay suspensions and the role of charge distribution in formation of cracks under electric field. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt describes Laponite® as a strongly anisotropic, disc-like platelet: approximately 25 nm in diameter but only 1 nm high. Its geometry is coupled to heterogeneous surface charge, with a negatively charged flat face and an edge (rim) that may carry positive or negative charge; at the reported pH 9.8, the rim remains positively charged. Although the passage does not provide a direct comparison with spherical particles or hBN, it indicates that platelet shape and charge distribution are important material features in crack formation under an electric field. Drying Laponite® in a rectangular cell with a DC field produces organized, hierarchical, tree-like crack patterns rather than an unspecified random crack network. Many cracks initially nucleate near the positive electrode, propagate toward the negative electrode, and merge with neighboring cracks, leaving fewer main cracks and branches oriented toward the positive electrode. The number of initial cracks and their merging rate depend on applied voltage, while box geometry also affects the number of trees and branching levels. Electric-field-driven cracks dissipate stress near the positive electrode early, suppressing ordinary desiccation cracks there. The excerpt therefore supports discussion of anisotropic clay platelets, electrostatic charge distribution, directional crack growth, and branching, but contains no evidence specifically about hBN or spherical-particle suspensions.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'ghosh2023studyofdesiccation pages 38-44'.

A Ghosh. Study of desiccation crack patterns in aqueous clay suspensions and the role of charge distribution in formation of cracks under electric field. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt identifies clay particles as anisotropic, plate-like colloids rather than spherical particles. Laponite® consists of disc-shaped phyllosilicate particles approximately 1 nm thick and 25 nm in diameter, while bentonite contains plate-shaped particles with a typical diameter of about 1 micrometre. This geometry creates a large flat surface relative to particle thickness and produces direction-dependent interactions. In Laponite®, the broad faces are negatively charged, whereas the rims carry pH-dependent positive charge; at the stated pH, the rims remain positively charged. These charge differences, together with overlapping electrical double layers, van der Waals attraction, and electrolyte-dependent repulsion, influence how particles associate, form gels, and organize before drying. The excerpt notes that concentrated Laponite® forms a nematic gel, indicating orientational ordering of the platelets, and that bentonite layers produce documented desiccation-crack patterns. Thus, the passage supplies material relevant to how platelet shape, surface charge, aggregation, and preferred orientation may affect drying structure and crack formation. However, it does not directly compare hBN or clay platelets with spherical particles, nor does it explicitly establish how platelet shape changes crack spacing, directionality, or propagation relative to spheres.

The excerpt identifies clay and Laponite—platelet-like colloidal materials—as important systems for studying drying crack formation, but it does not provide a direct explanation of how platelet or anisotropic particle shape changes cracking relative to spherical particles. The cited works indicate that drying crack networks in Laponite and clay are examined in terms of crack formation, topology, interface area, thickness, and repeated wetting–drying cycles. The references to colloid science and clay colloid chemistry suggest that particle interactions, surface charge, dispersion state, and colloidal structure are relevant factors alongside geometry. For a comparison with spherical particles, the excerpt points generally toward studies of cracking in colloidal films and capillary shrinkage, but it does not report specific results for spherical particles. Likewise, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is not mentioned in the supplied pages. Therefore, this material supports the relevance of platelet clay/Laponite systems to desiccation-crack research, while leaving the specific mechanisms—such as orientation, stacking, anisotropic contact networks, or differences in crack spacing and morphology versus spherical particles—to the cited original studies or other sources.

Include: 1) Excessive coating thickness exceeding critical cracking thickness (most likely), 2) Non-absorptive fired BN substrate preventing solvent wicking and causing rapid film consolidation, 3) Rapid drying in fume hood (forced airflow over volatile acetone/ethanol solvents), 4) Poor spray technique (insufficient shaking, pooling in deep crucible, wrong distance), 5) B2O3/borate residue from fired coat creating weak hygroscopic boundary layer, 6) Locally doubled thickness at old coat/bare graphite boundary"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Rank | Cause | Mechanism | Supporting Evidence | Likelihood |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Excessive coating thickness exceeding the critical cracking thickness | Capillary pressure contracts the particle network; adhesion to the crucible constrains in-plane shrinkage, producing tensile stress. Crack resistance decreases as film thickness increases, so heavy passes, pooled bottom deposits, or multiple coats can cross the critical thickness. | The Singh–Tirumkudulu model predicts that maximum crack-free thickness increases with particle size and modulus and decreases with solvent surface tension. Applying this spherical-particle model to hBN platelets is only an estimate. ZYP-related tests found greater cracking with two coats and full-surface cracking with three hand-applied coats. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000005) | **Very high** |
| 2 | Different absorption or wicking behavior of a fired BN substrate | **Hypothesis requiring verification:** a fired BN surface may absorb less solvent than bare porous graphite, leaving more liquid and solids at the surface and allowing the new layer to consolidate as a thicker, strongly constrained film. Conversely, a porous old coating could wick solvent downward and accelerate consolidation from below. | Literature supports substrate constraint and nonuniform consolidation, but does not establish the direction or magnitude of solvent transport for this product on fired BN. A clean-graphite-versus-fired-coat coupon test is needed. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | **High, but mechanism uncertain** |
| 3 | Rapid, nonuniform drying in the fume hood | Forced airflow over volatile acetone and ethanol increases mass transfer and can produce edge-first or top-first consolidation, lateral drying fronts, and shrinkage gradients. Capillary pressure is not directly determined by evaporation rate, but rapid, uneven drying changes where and when stress develops. | Particulate-coating studies document edge-first drying, nonuniform consolidation, and worsening cracking under more aggressive drying conditions. Direct evidence for this exact aerosol in a 0.3–0.5 m/s hood is unavailable. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | **High** |
| 4 | Poor spray technique: insufficient shaking, excessive wetness, wrong distance, or pooling | Settled BN can cause nonuniform solids delivery; close spraying, slow movement, weak atomization, and overspray into the bottom-wall corner of a deep crucible can produce wet, locally thick deposits. These areas store more elastic energy during constrained drying. | The thickness consequence is strongly supported by coating literature, but these specific operating errors remain unverified because shaking time, spray distance, pass count, flash time, and can condition were not recorded. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031) | **High** |
| 5 | B2O3 or borate residue creating a weak, hygroscopic boundary layer | hBN can oxidize from roughly 800 °C in air to form B2O3. B2O3 is hygroscopic and may react with moisture to form metaboric or orthoboric acid; residue could alter wetting, absorb moisture, redistribute during recoating, and weaken adhesion. | Oxidation and hygroscopicity are supported, but significant B2O3 formation during an argon run depends on oxygen leakage and prior air exposure. Its presence on this crucible remains unconfirmed. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020) | **Medium** |
| 6 | Locally doubled thickness at old-coat edges or bare-graphite crescents | Recoating without complete stripping can double film thickness over retained regions, while recesses and crescent edges collect additional spray. Abrupt thickness, porosity, and stiffness changes concentrate stress and can initiate cracks or delamination. | Critical-thickness theory and evidence that substrate steps act as crack initiators support this mechanism, but the condition of the old underlayer was not documented. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031) | **Medium to high** |

Scaling to R=2.5 \u00b5m platelets: hmax ~ R^(3/2) so increase by factor (2500/100)^1.5 \u2248 125, but also \u03b3 is lower (22 vs 72) so additional factor of (72/22)^0.5 \u2248 1.8. This gives rough estimate hmax \u2248 17.5 \u00d7 125 \u00d7 1.8 / (correction for lower effective G and \u03c6) \u2248 several hundred \u00b5m to >1 mm if using full single-crystal G. BUT effective G for loose platelet packing might be 100-1000\u00d7 lower than single crystal, reducing hmax by 10-30\u00d7. Conclude that estimated hmax is probably 50-500 \u00b5m with large uncertainty - meaning 50-150 \u00b5m is plausibly near or above the critical thickness."}

| Effective shear modulus of drying platelet network | \(G_{\mathrm{eff}}\) | **Estimate:** 0.1–1 GPa | Assumed for sensitivity analysis, not measured for Spray II. | Final packing fraction | \(\phi\) | **Estimate:** 0.40–0.55 for platelets; sphere reference \(\phi_{\mathrm{rcp}}\approx0.64\) | Platelet orientation, agglomeration, polydispersity, and organoclay can shift packing and pore-throat size. | Modulus correction relative to a stiff reference network | \(f_G\) | **Estimate:** approximately 1/10 to 1/32 for a 100–1000-fold lower effective modulus | Because \(h_{\max}\propto G^{1/2}\), weak contacts and low binder content can reduce the uncorrected result to approximately 0.13–0.40 mm before additional platelet-packing, adhesion, defect, and thickness-nonuniformity corrections. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Step | Action | Details and parameters | Rationale |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Strip failed or uncertain old coating | Remove the crucible from service. Gently dry-scrape with a clean wooden or polymer tool, followed by a nonmetallic abrasive pad approved by the crucible manufacturer. Remove loose fired coating, lifted edges, skull residue, and metal or oxide contamination. If permitted, wipe sparingly with reagent-grade IPA on a lint-free cloth; never soak or use water. Blow clean with dry, oil-free N₂ or Ar. | A cracked or weak underlayer cannot support a reliable recoat. Retained coating creates thickness steps and weak interfaces that can initiate cracks. Avoiding water limits moisture retention and hydration of possible hygroscopic B₂O₃ residue. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |
| 2 | Prepare and dry the surface | Inspect under bright light and 5–10× magnification. Require clean, dry, uniformly textured graphite without glossy metal, waxy residue, loose powder, or abrupt old-coat edges. **Estimate:** after IPA, allow at least 30 min of ventilated evaporation. Optionally warm the empty crucible to 60–80°C for 10–30 min, then cool to the label-approved application temperature in a dry location. | Residual solvent or moisture can change wetting and drying. A uniform surface reduces local variations in constraint and deposited thickness. The temperature and time are estimates, not verified Momentive instructions. |
| 3 | Condition and shake the aerosol | Stabilize the can and crucible at room temperature. Shake for the label-specified period. If the current label gives no time, **2 min is a provisional estimate**; reshake intermittently during use. Clear and test the nozzle on a weighed graphite coupon. Do not use a damaged, overheated, chilled, nearly empty, sputtering, or poorly atomizing can. | Dense BN platelets can settle. Inadequate redispersion can produce changing solids concentration and a coarse, wet spray. A coupon identifies abnormal atomization before the crucible is coated. |
| 4 | Apply the first light pass | Spray in an approved ignition-controlled enclosure or fume hood suitable for acetone, ethanol, and LPG vapors; never spray in unventilated still air. Follow the label distance. If none is stated, **20–25 cm is an experimental coupon-test estimate**. Use a quick sweeping motion and rotate or tilt the crucible to prevent accumulation at the bottom-wall corner. Deposit a translucent mist rather than a wet continuous layer. | Ventilation is required for the flammable solvents and propellant. A thin, uniform pass limits capillary stress and local exceedance of the critical cracking thickness. Deep crucibles are particularly susceptible to pooling. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031) |
| 5 | Flash between passes | Maintain safe vapor extraction but shield the wet surface from a direct, asymmetric high-velocity draft. Wait until the coating is uniformly matte and no longer visibly wet. **Estimate:** begin coupon trials with 2–3 min between passes and extend the interval if the bottom or corner remains wet. Do not tightly cover a solvent-wet crucible. | Rapid or spatially uneven evaporation can cause edge-first consolidation and shrinkage gradients. Flashing also prevents successive passes from merging into one thick wet layer. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000029) |
| 6 | Apply the minimum additional coating | Add a second light pass only where required. Use **2–3 light passes as a provisional coupon-test maximum**, not as verified Momentive guidance. **Estimated trial target:** 20–50 µm total dry thickness, verified by coupon mass gain rather than pass count. Stop if the film becomes wet, glossy, rough, or visibly crazed. | BN release coatings can work as very thin layers, whereas excess multilayer thickness promotes cracking. Tests involving another BN coating found greater cracking with two hand-applied coats and full-surface cracking with three; this is cautionary, not product-specific. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000028) |
| 7 | Dry under controlled ventilation | Continue extraction until the flammable-vapor hazard has passed while avoiding a direct draft across the crucible mouth. If site procedures permit, then transfer the crucible to a clean, dry, low-draft enclosure. **Estimate:** dry for at least 30–60 min at room temperature or gently warm the empty crucible to 50–60°C after vapors have been exhausted. Never place a freshly sprayed, solvent-bearing crucible directly into a hot oven. | Controlled drying reduces lateral fronts and top-to-bottom drying gradients while preserving fire safety. Greater film thickness and aggressive drying conditions can increase particulate-coating cracking. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000029) |
| 8 | Conduct an empty-crucible low-temperature bake if approved | Use a separately ventilated oven or furnace rated for the anticipated solvent and VOC load. **Provisional estimate:** ramp the empty crucible slowly to 100–120°C, hold for 30–60 min, and cool in dry air or inert gas. Do not use 200°C without written confirmation from Momentive and the crucible manufacturer. | A controlled bake can remove retained solvent before furnace installation. This schedule is an engineering estimate because verified Spray II bake instructions were not available in the reviewed evidence. |
| 9 | Perform organic burnout before charging metal | Do not burn out the coating with metal present. Under an approved furnace procedure, heat the empty coated crucible under flowing inert gas with safe exhaust and gas monitoring. **Provisional example requiring validation:** ramp at no more than 1–2°C/min to 200°C, hold 30–60 min, then ramp at no more than 1–2°C/min to 500°C and hold until the exhaust is clear and stable. Smoke signifies continuing decomposition, not successful completion. | Empty burnout prevents decomposition products from contaminating the charge and permits shutdown if the coating smokes, blisters, or spalls. Organic additives can mitigate drying defects but introduce burnout risks. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000027) |
| 10 | Inspect and accept or reject | Inspect after ambient drying and again after the empty bake or burnout. **Pass:** thin, uniformly matte-white coating without polygonal cracks, long cracks, pinholes exposing graphite, curled edges, blisters, powder piles, loose flakes, or transfer during a very light clean-glove touch at a sacrificial rim area. **Reject and restrip:** any mud cracking, lifting, flaking, exposed graphite in a melt-contact area, or crack extending into the graphite. | A cracked low-binder coating can expose graphite and release flakes into the melt or nozzle. Because Al–carbon reactions are thermodynamically possible and BN supplies the nonwetting barrier, visible cracking should be treated as failure unless a controlled validation program proves otherwise. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026) |


*Table: A conservative procedure for stripping, recoating, drying, and inspecting the graphite crucible. Unverified process values are marked as estimates requiring coupon tests and manufacturer approval.*

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer. The charge is induction-melted in a graphite
crucible (grade not yet confirmed, probably a fine-grained isostatic graphite) whose interior is sprayed
with a boron nitride release coating, then pushed by argon pressure through a bottom hBN nozzle. The alloy
is nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 (Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%) melted at 1300 C under argon, in charges of
0.86-1.08 kg.

The coating is Momentive Technologies "Boron Nitride Spray II, High-Temperature Release Coating"
(material number 2111750, 13 oz / 369 g aerosol can). Its SDS, as we read it (please verify), lists
hexagonal BN in ethanol and acetone, LPG (propane/butane) propellant and 1-5% organoclay (a
bentonite-based rheology additive), so the dry film is BN platelets with very little binder. Momentive
rates a can for roughly 100 sq ft.

History:
- Coat 1 (before a 27 Oct run): sprayed onto the clean, bare graphite and left to dry. It did NOT crack.
  It was not baked before use: the chamber filled with smoke at about 500 C during the first heat-up,
  with the metal charge already loaded (binder burnout in the furnace).
- After that run a thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling it
  pulled away crescent-shaped patches of the BN coat, leaving bare graphite. A second run used the
  crucible with those bare patches, without recoating.
- Coat 2 (30 Oct): the crucible was re-sprayed with the same product and left to dry in a laboratory fume
  hood. When the operator came back, the coat was cracked. It cracked at room temperature during drying,
  before any heating. We do not yet know: whether the old fired coat was fully stripped or the new coat
  went over it (or over the patch edges); how many passes, how far from the surface, or how long the can
  was shaken; whether the crucible had just been wiped with isopropanol (our recoat notes say to wipe with
  IPA and never water); the room humidity; the crack pattern (polygonal "mud-crack" network, curling
  flakes, or single long cracks); and whether only the coat cracked or the graphite too.

Please answer as a literature review with numbers and sources (papers with DOIs, manufacturer data sheets
and application instructions). Mark every estimate as an estimate and show its inputs. Start with a
short ranked list of the most likely causes, then cover:

1. Mechanism. Explain drying cracks in sprayed particulate coatings: capillary pressure in the drying
   particle network, constraint by the substrate, and the critical cracking thickness (for example Chiu
   et al. 1993 in J. Am. Ceram. Soc.; Routh and Russel; Tirumkudulu and Russel 2005; Singh and
   Tirumkudulu 2007; Lee and Routh; work on films of platelet particles). How do particle size, packing, platelet shape and
   orientation (hBN platelets of about 0.5-10 um), a few percent clay or organic binder, solvent surface
   tension (acetone and ethanol, about 22-23 mN/m) and drying rate change the critical thickness? Estimate
   the critical cracking thickness of a hBN-platelet film with 1-5% organoclay, and compare it with the
   wet and dry thickness an aerosol deposits per pass. How many grams of spray per square centimetre give
   what dry thickness? Is a dry BN film of 50-150 um above or below the critical thickness?
2. Substrate and history. Why would the same spray crack on a crucible that had already been coated and
   fired, when it did not crack on bare graphite? Consider: a porous, binder-free fired BN layer (or
   residual borate or B2O3) that wicks the solvent and consolidates the new film from below; poor adhesion
   or a weak boundary layer under the new film; locally doubled thickness where new spray overlaps old
   coat or fills the bare crescents; residues from the skull (Al2O3, metal, reaction products); solvent or
   moisture left in porous graphite or in the old coat after an IPA wipe; hydration of B2O3 or borate in
   the fired coat to boric acid; and porosity or surface texture of the graphite. Which of these are
   supported by literature or vendor guidance, and which are speculation?
3. Drying conditions. What does strong airflow (a fume hood face velocity of about 0.3-0.5 m/s) do to an
   acetone/ethanol BN film: faster evaporation, skin formation, lateral drying fronts, evaporative cooling
   below the dew point with water condensing into the film ("blushing"), and non-uniform drying in a deep
   cup? Would slower drying (still air, a lid, or gentle warming) avoid cracking? Quantify where you can.
4. Spray technique. Effects of insufficient shaking (BN settles quickly), spray distance, can and part
   temperature, a nearly empty can (lower propellant pressure giving a wetter, coarser spray), spraying
   into a deep cylindrical crucible (overspray pooling on the bottom and in the corner), and the number of
   passes and the flash time between them. Collect vendor instructions with numbers from Momentive, ZYP
   Coatings (BN Lubricoat and Hardcoat aerosols), Saint-Gobain (Combat), Henze (HeBoCoat), 3M and others,
   especially statements that cracking, flaking or peeling means the coat is too thick, and their advice
   on recoating over an existing or fired coat versus stripping it first.
5. Momentive Boron Nitride Spray II specifically. What do Momentive's technical data sheet, SDS and
   application notes say about composition, binder, thickness per coat, drying time, whether to bake
   before contact with metal, maximum use temperature in air and in inert gas, and recoating? Is another
   product (Momentive's water-based BN paints, or a hard-coat BN with an inorganic binder) better suited
   to repeated recoating of a graphite crucible for an aluminum-containing copper melt at 1300 C?
6. Consequences and diagnosis. How do you tell drying mud-cracks in the coat from cracks in the graphite
   (for example thermal-shock cracks that show through) or old cracks telegraphing through the new coat?
   Is a finely mud-cracked but adherent BN release coat acceptable for a 1300 C aluminum bronze melt, or
   does the melt penetrate the cracks, reach the graphite (Al4C3, carbon pickup, skull adhesion) and lift
   flakes into the melt and the nozzle? Must it be stripped?
7. Fix. Give a step-by-step strip, recoat, dry and inspect procedure for this product on a graphite
   crucible that avoids cracking: how to strip a cracked or fired BN coat without water, surface
   preparation, passes, thickness per pass and in total, flash time, where and how to dry, an optional
   low-temperature warm-up and the burnout or bake before the first melt, and pass/fail inspection
   criteria. Also propose a small coupon test (graphite offcuts) that would identify which factor caused
   the cracking, for example clean graphite versus a fired coat, fume-hood draft versus still air, and
   one versus three versus six passes, with weighing to estimate thickness.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this complex question about BN coating cracking on graphite crucibles for aluminum bronze atomization.

Abstract:
Cracking of suspensions during drying is a common problem. While additives, e.g. binders and surfactants, can mitigate this problem, some applications, such as printing conductive pastes or sintering green bodies, do not lend themselves to the use of additives. Capillary suspensions provide an alternative formulation without additives. In this work, we use simultaneous stress and weight measurements to investigate the influence of formulation and drying conditions. Capillary suspensions dry more homogeneously and with lower peak stresses, leading to an increased robustness against cracking compared. An increase in dry film porosity is not the key driver for the stress reduction. Instead, the capillary bridges, which create strong particle networks, resist the stress. Increasing the relative humidity enhances this effect, even for pure suspensions. While lower boiling point secondary liquids, e.g. water, persist for very long times during drying, higher boiling point liquids offer further potential to tune the the drying process.

Abstract:
Thin films of polymer coatings have important industrial applications ranging from paints and coatings to pharmaceuticals. In many applications, the coatings are obtained by applying thin films of dilute polymer solutions, wherein the solvent evaporates to leave behind a thin polymer film. In some cases, the thin films may crack due to shrinkage stresses developed during drying. While a number of studies have focused on the stress development, the phenomenon of cracking in polymer films is not fully investigated. In the present work, thin films of a silicone polymer solution were cast on substrates of varying Young's moduli and investigated for cracking as a function of film thickness and substrate modulus. Micro-Raman spectroscopy measurements show that thin films dry uniformly while thick films form a skin at the top surface leading to slow drying rates. Transverse stresses were measured using the cantilever technique and related to the extent of cracking in the film. We investigated the influence of substrate rigidity on the cracking behavior and found that decreasing the stiffness of the substrate increases the extent of cracking.

Abstract:
<jats:p>We report a systematic investigation of GME (1-glyceryl monooleyl ether) self-assembly of TiO₂–water–butanediol quaternary colloidal suspensions and its consequences for crack formation during film drying. Because 1,4-butanediol has a boiling point of ~230°C and a vapour pressure orders of magnitude below that of water, drying progressively enriches the GME–butanediol–water phase in both co-solvent and surfactant rather than depleting it of a volatile additive. Cross-polarised optical microscopy (POM) established that lamellar or hexagonal lyotropic liquid-crystalline (LC) phases form at ≥2 wt% GME in butanediol:water 1:20 mixtures, and at ≥2 wt% GME in 3:7 mixtures. UNIFAC-based drying-path simulations confirmed that water evaporates preferentially, predicting that 3:7 BDO/H₂O formulations at ≥2 wt% GME cross into the lamellar LC window when ≈72 ± 4% of the initial water remains. Critical cracking thickness (hᴄᴄᴛ) measurements on TiO₂ films (≈200 nm, 3.5 vol%) demonstrated a 2.3-fold increase from 17.5 ± 0.6 µm (additive-free control) to 41.4 ± 2.9 µm at 3:7 BDO/3 wt% GME at 25°C (p < 0.001, one-way ANOVA). The enhancement is primarily LC-mediated: the apparent shear modulus Gₐₚₚ of the LC phase (exp(0.71ϕf)) elevates the Tirumkudulu–Russel fracture-resistance prefactor by a factor of ≈1.7× (model R² = 0.993). Residual butanediol in dried films (9.4 ± 0.6 wt% at the 3:7/2 wt% GME condition) contributes a secondary plasticisation effect (r² = 0.62 vs. r² = 0.91 for the LC contribution). Isomer comparison confirmed that 1,4-butanediol (hᴄᴄᴛ = 34.0 µm) outperforms 1,3-butanediol (29.7 µm) and 2,3-butanediol (27.2 µm), consistent with the linear backbone geometry of 1,4-BDO favouring GME lamellar packing. These results demonstrate a low-volatility, low-VOC additive route to crack-free thick particulate coatings and offer a mechanistic framework for non-volatile co-solvent–amphiphile systems in particulate film drying.</jats:p>

Abstract The aim of this study is to assess the effectiveness of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) coatings to enhance the corrosion resistance of metals as well as evaluate their crucial toxicological impacts on both the environment and human health. Organic coatings are extensively applied in the field of protecting metals against corrosion. They are preferred as corrosion inhibitors due to their carbonyl and hydroxyl group content, but they have drawbacks regarding brittleness, porosity, and oxidation susceptibility. In this review, we mainly focused on the synthesis, properties, and applications of hBN coatings and emphasized the way to improve corrosion resistance in metals and alloys. Furthermore, our discussion demonstrated that the boron nitride nanosheet (BNNS) coatings significantly improve corrosion resistance, hydrophobicity, and crack mitigation properties. The researchers achieved reduced coating porosity and enhanced protection against corrosive media by effectively dispersing BNNS in organic resin. This study also determines the protective mechanism of BNNS composite coatings against corrosion. Moreover, we addressed the impact of BBNS synthesis and its physicochemical properties on the environment and organisms. Finally, suggestions are made for future research and the sustainability of industrial use to broaden the scope of applications for BNNS composite coating.
